title: OpenTLP protocol family
description:
The front matter of one protocol family page — the wire format shared by every device whose `protocol.family` names it.

A device page says which family a printer belongs to and what it is; this says how to talk to that family, in enough structured detail that writing a driver is transcription rather than reverse engineering.

What it does NOT try to be is executable. A declarative format rich enough to generate a working driver for a protocol with handshakes, acknowledgements and flow control would be a programming language, and a worse one than the languages people already use. The fields here capture the parameters that are easy to get wrong and impossible to notice — bit order, checksum polynomial, compression window — and `conformance` points at vectors that prove an implementation right.

The same rule applies as everywhere else: every field is a checkable claim, and an absent one means unknown.

id.description: Family slug, matching `protocol.family` on device pages. Permanent: drivers and device entries both key on it.

also_known_as.description: Names other projects use for the same protocol. Worth recording: half the difficulty in this field is two communities describing one wire format in different words.

based_on.description: A published standard this family extends, e.g. 'ESC/POS', 'TSPL'. Where one exists, prefer it as the reference — a standard cannot contaminate an implementation's licence, and one implementation covers every manufacturer that speaks it.

acknowledges.description:
Whether the printer confirms what it receives.

The single most consequential fact about a family. Where this is false a malformed packet produces silence rather than an error, there is no way to distinguish a rejected job from a successful one except by looking at the paper, and every driver bug costs a roll of labels to find.

commands.description: Known opcodes. Partial lists are useful and expected — nobody maps a whole family at once.

implementations.description: Where to read a working driver for this family, and under what licence. The licence matters: a reader may take protocol facts from any of these, but code only from those whose terms allow it.

status.description: 'verified' means an independent implementation built from this description drives the hardware — ideally proven against `conformance` vectors.

framing.description: Packet structure. Getting any one of these wrong produces a packet the printer discards, and on a family that does not acknowledge, discards silently.

prefix.description: Leading bytes of every packet, lowercase hex, space separated.

layout.description: One line naming the fields in order, e.g. 'prefix, command, length (u16le), payload, crc8'. Prose because packet layouts vary more than any fixed structure would capture, and a reader needs the order more than a parser does.

covers.description: What the length counts. Ambiguous in every capture and wrong in half of all first attempts.

checksum.description: Enough to reproduce the algorithm exactly. A CRC named only by width is not reproducible — the polynomial, the initial value and the reflection settings are all free parameters, and every combination produces plausible-looking bytes.

raster.description: How a bitmap becomes bytes. These four fields — bit order, polarity, padding, compression — account for most of the images that print as noise, mirrored, or inverted.

bit_order.description: Which end of a byte holds the leftmost pixel. Wrong choice mirrors every 8-pixel group.

polarity.description: Wrong choice prints the negative, and wastes a great deal of a roll doing it.

row_padding.description: Whether each row starts on a byte boundary. 'byte' is near-universal; with 'none' rows run together and the image shears.

width_unit.description: What the width field in a raster header counts. A common off-by-eight.

window_bits.description: zlib window size as the exponent. Firmware with a small buffer often requires a smaller window than the default 15, and a stream compressed with the wrong one is still valid zlib — it simply prints nothing. Visible in the two-byte header.

header_bytes.description: The stream header the printer expects, as a check on the settings above.

flow.description: How fast data may be pushed, and how the printer says stop.

max_write_bytes.description: Largest single write the family reliably accepts. Often well below the MTU a device will negotiate; oversized writes are dropped without complaint.

control.description: 'notify-pause' — the printer sends a byte sequence on its notify characteristic when its buffer fills. Ignoring it costs bands of missing rows on long jobs.

payload.description: One line describing the payload, e.g. 'u8 density 1-15'.

status.description: 'confirmed' means the effect was observed on hardware, not guessed from a capture's context.

conformance.description:
Golden vectors: known inputs and the exact bytes they must produce.

The only way to prove a protocol implementation correct without owning the hardware, and the reason a port can be trusted at all. An implementation that reproduces the vectors byte for byte is right about framing, checksums, bit order and compression settings simultaneously.

licence.description: SPDX id of the vectors. They are usually part of a project and carry its terms.

covers.description: Which parts of the protocol the vectors exercise.

module.description: Path or module name within that project.
